prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Context: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen seeks increased National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. Adverse weather causes approximately 70% of US operational delays; convection, winds, turbulence, snow/ice, and visibility/low ceilings constrain operations through automation, policy, and procedural limitations.
Elements/actors: FAA; FAA traffic managers; FAA air traffic control system; controllers; aircraft; aircraft/flight operators; general public; National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA); industry; other air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders. NASA’s 2015 survey identified weather-related en route delays/interruptions as the most significant, costly issue.
Proposed systems: NASA’s Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) project integrates ground-/aircraft-based technologies and decision aids to continuously seek efficient weather-avoidance routes and respond rapidly to weather changes and associated Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs). Enhancements target en route airspace and enable continued en route and arrival metering during weather. Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR), a subset, primarily addresses cruise flight. DWR uses existing air traffic weather, airspace, and traffic data; navigation, surveillance, communication, and digital-network improvements; and existing ATM automation. Intended benefits: time, fuel, cost, and environmental savings.
Current interactions: TMIs divert aircraft safely around adverse weather and meter traffic when demand exceeds air traffic control’s safe-separation capacity. FAA traffic managers identify forecast significant-convection regions as Flow Constrained Area (FCA) and may implement Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), also called Playbook routes. Routes are identified 2–8 hours before predicted constraint development, allowing traffic managers/operators to prepare and assign resources. Forecast uncertainty and adjacent-sector capacity limitations cause geographically/temporally conservative diversions, minimizing difficult subsequent changes. Existing automation does not notify managers when constraints change and avoidance routes become unnecessary, prolonging inefficient routing.
Conditions: fair versus adverse weather, especially significant convection; not formal modes. No explicit normative requirements or detailed item interfaces specified.

Document units:
U0025: Additionally, these large-scale rerouting actions also tend to use a static approach by finding the best compromise between weather avoidance, controller workload, and route efficiency...prioritized in that order.
U0026: Due to the difficulty in applying changes, aircraft often remain on conservative routes which are not required for weather avoidance.
U0027: Modifying those routes for aircraft already in flight requires a lot of coordination and can be time-consuming.
U0028: And there is no automation in the current system to help operators identify workable opportunities for time and fuel- saving corrections to weather avoidance routes that have become stale due to changing weather and forecast uncertainty.
U0029: Air traffic controllers, airline dispatchers and pilots can manually identify and request or amend these conservative routes as things progress to improve efficiency.
U0030: However, the associated workload to do so is very high at a time when controllers and dispatchers are very busy.
U0031: Consequently, aircraft often remain on circuitous routes long after the driving constraint is gone thereby incurring costly and unnecessary delays, and fuel consumption.
U0032: Airline flight dispatchers must file flight plans at least 45 min before push-back from the gate using their best available weather forecasts, but in practice flight plans are typically filed 1-2 hours before take-off.
U0033: When SWAP routes are in effect, dispatchers determine which SWAP routes are applicable to a flight’s planned route of flight and file a revised route accordingly.
U0034: Efforts have been made to apply more tactical operational tools to account for changes.
U0035: A good example is the Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP), which allows operators to file multiple routes on a single flight plan based on the amount of departure delay to which the flight is subjected and the operators associated preferences for that flight.
U0036: Although this provides a level of improvement over traditional single-route flight plans and rerouting procedures, it is still strategic in nature.
U0037: Therefore it provides no improvement in efficiency, flexibility and responsiveness to changes after departure.
U0038: Additionally, flight crews lack the tools to identify more efficient routes that will avoid congested airspace or conflicts with other aircraft.
U0039: And although they can identify more efficient trajectories using flight management systems and weather radar, they are unable to see convective weather anywhere beyond the limits of their on-board radar.
